summaries.Q1519002: In 1824 the painter and collector François-Xavier Fabre offered to give his collections to his native city, on condition that a museum be built to house them. The city bought the hôtel de Massilian in 1825 and the museum opened on 3 December 1828. Closed from 2003 to 2007, it grew from 3,000 to 9,000 m2 of exhibition space.
summaries.Q3330631: Housed since 1992 in the former hôtel des Trésoriers de France, rue Jacques Cœur, it displays the collections gathered since 1833 by the Société archéologique de Montpellier: Montpellier faience, carved capitals, medieval tableware. The museum has been closed until further notice since 2016.
summaries.Q3373119: This 650 m2 neo-Renaissance building was erected in 1891 by the city architect Léopold Carlier for the Cercle des étudiants. In financial difficulty, the latter left the premises to the city in 1905, which passed them on to local societies: the name pavillon populaire dates from that time. Since 2001 it has been a municipal venue devoted to photography.
summaries.Q104617429: Founded in 1879, this astronomical observatory stands in the very heart of the jardin des plantes and is attached to the faculty of medicine. That same year its dome received the Foucault telescope, built in 1877 at the Paris Observatory by William Eichens to Foucault’s designs.
summaries.Q3298462: In 1181 the lord Guilhem VIII authorised “any man, whoever he may be and wherever he may come from” to run a school of medicine in Montpellier; in 1220 a papal legate granted the universitas medicorum its first statutes. Since 1795 the faculty has occupied the former collège Saint-Benoît built by Urban V, which had become the episcopal palace in 1536.
summaries.Q1736197: The chapel of the Saint-Benoît monastery founded in 1364 by Pope Urban V, it was raised to cathedral status in 1536, when the episcopal see left Maguelone. Its massive porch, with two cylindrical piers, is one of the few medieval elements preserved: in 1567 a Protestant assault brought down a tower, and the building with it.
summaries.Q2886965: The name comes from the money changers’ tables set up in the Middle Ages around the church of Sainte-Marie, demolished from 1794 onwards. The title was transferred in 1802 to the former chapel of the Jesuit college, built from 1707 to 1748 under the direction of Jean Giral. Pius XII raised it to a minor basilica in 1939.
summaries.Q3584279: Dedicated to the saint who healed plague victims and was born in the city, this neo-Gothic church was built from 1860 to 1868 by the municipal architect Jean Cassan, on the site of the church of Saint-Paul destroyed in 1622. It has remained unfinished: the two side spires planned above the bell tower were never raised.
summaries.Q56602235: A church stood here as early as the 13th century; destroyed in 1568, rebuilt in 1665, it was pulled down in 1865 after a report warning that it was unsafe. The neo-Gothic building by Jean Cassan that replaced it rises to 69 metres, the tallest monument in the city centre. Deconsecrated in 1986 and turned into the Carré Sainte-Anne in 1991, it reopened on 27 May 2025.
summaries.Q19815207: For nearly six hundred years it was the chapel of the Mercedarians, an order devoted to ransoming Christians enslaved in Muslim lands. The enlargement of the place Royale du Peyrou led to the demolition of their convent in 1740; the new church, begun in 1741 by Antoine Vier, was consecrated in 1748.
summaries.Q3581345: Built from 1699 to 1702 by Augustin-Charles d’Aviler in the faubourg de la Saunerie, it replaced a church of the same name destroyed in the wars of religion. Closed by the revolutionary section in 1793 and sold at auction, it was bought back by the faithful and returned to worship in 1801. Enlarged in 1836 and again in 1895, it has kept only its façade intact.
summaries.Q2957097: Known as the chapel of the White Penitents, it was burnt and then destroyed by the Huguenots in 1562 and 1568. Too close to the rampart to be rebuilt, its ruins served as an open-air cemetery for more than fifty years. Returned to the confraternity in 1623, it was consecrated on Christmas night 1624 and received a painted coffered ceiling from 1671 to 1691.
summaries.Q3001757: Six nuns from Pézenas settled here in 1641 to teach poor girls, in a monastery rebuilt in 1657 by Jean Bonnassier. The place became a prison, a barracks, a women’s prison from 1825 to 1934, a Gestapo interrogation site under the Occupation, then a barracks again until 1986. It houses the national choreographic centre.
summaries.Q96472208: This 12th-century Jewish ritual bath is cut into the sandstone, about five metres below the present street. Its basin is fed by the water table, without any hand touching the water. Dismantled after the expulsion of the Jews in 1306, it served as a well and then as a coal cellar before being rediscovered in the early 1980s.
summaries.Q968684: The theatre opened in 1755 was damaged by a fire in 1785, rebuilt identically and back in use in 1788. The fire of the night of 5 to 6 April 1881 destroyed it completely. The present building, inaugurated in 1888, is the work of Joseph-Marie Cassien-Bernard, a pupil of Charles Garnier; its Italian-style auditorium seats 1,200.
summaries.Q3438008: Beneath the concert hall survives the crypt of the Franciscans, whose church was consecrated in 1264. Charles Bonaparte, father of Napoleon I, who died in Montpellier in 1785, was first buried there. The city’s first garage in 1903 and a cinema in 1927, the place became the Rockstore in 1986: its red Cadillac is inspired by the first Hard Rock Café in New York.
summaries.Q3145663: The surgeon François de Lapeyronie bequeathed part of his fortune to give Montpellier an anatomy theatre like the one at the collège Saint-Côme in Paris. Built from 1747 to 1757 to plans by Jean-Antoine Giral, the building combines the surgeons’ meeting room with the amphitheatre at the far end of the courtyard.
summaries.Q2998146: A congress centre designed by Claude Vasconi, the Corum is recognisable by its roof of pink Finnish granite slabs. Its first phase was delivered in 1989, the opéra Berlioz and its 2,000 seats in 1990. Its heliport has been used only once, for François Mitterrand’s visit at the inauguration.
summaries.Q2092877: Twenty-six metres high, it is one of the last remnants of the twenty-five towers of the commune clôture, the city’s medieval wall. Raised for an astronomical observatory completed in 1745, it was used in December 1783 by the physicist Lenormand to test his parachute with animals, before a crowd that included Joseph Montgolfier.
summaries.Q3533649: Originally twenty-nine metres high, this tower of the medieval wall lost four when its ditch was filled in in 1778. Its defensive role abandoned in 1592, it served as a dwelling, a prison and an asylum, then received the municipal archives in 1886. The people of Montpellier attached to it a prediction of Nostradamus: the city would perish when the pines disappeared.
summaries.Q2849122: Built from 1624 to 1627 on the orders of Louis XIII to watch over a city and a region with a large Protestant population, the stronghold was raised to plans by Jean de Beins and had four bastions. Now the Joffre barracks, it houses a lycée whose first term began on 1 October 1948.
summaries.Q3361016: Here stood the fortress of the Guilhems, lords of Montpellier, demolished in 1577 during the wars of Religion. The Cour des comptes, aides et finances moved onto its ruins in 1629. As the building was badly dilapidated in 1839, it was replaced by the present neoclassical palace, built from 1846 to 1853 to plans by Charles Abric.
summaries.Q3146252: Built around 1448 for Jacques Cœur by Simon de Beaujeu, it received sovereigns visiting Languedoc. Acquired in 1632 by the trésoriers et grands voyers de France, it was almost entirely rebuilt from 1676 onwards: no exterior façade, but a courtyard with two superimposed colonnades. It has housed the musée languedocien since 1992.
summaries.Q22953952: A private mansion in Montpellier, in the Hérault department. Its façade and roof facing the square have been listed as historic monuments since 23 March 1943.
summaries.Q3145519: A Montpellier folie built from 1752 to 1760 by Jean Antoine Giral for Henri Haguenot, dean of the university, who was over seventy when he decided to have this country house built below the Peyrou. Façades, roofs and garden have been classified as historic monuments since 1963.
summaries.Q17354824: A private mansion in Montpellier, in the Hérault department. The building has been listed as a historic monument since 28 July 1945.
summaries.Q22953941: In the hands of the David de Fizes family from around 1640, this mansion in the Écusson sets against an austere façade a monumental doorway dated 1665, whose upper decoration of cut leatherwork shows two captives back to back. Its loggia staircase is one of the first in Montpellier to have had a wrought-iron railing.
summaries.Q17354817: A private mansion in Montpellier, in the Hérault department. The building has been listed as a historic monument since 3 March 1954.
summaries.Q3145855: A private mansion at 26 rue de l’Aiguillerie, in Montpellier. The building has been listed as a historic monument since 18 October 1944.
summaries.Q17354818: Owned by the City of Montpellier, this mansion housed a leisure centre and a municipal crèche from 1984 to 2025, which had to leave the premises after lead was found in the building. Closed to the public on 1 March 2025, it faces several years of works. A first listing as a historic monument dates from 1944.
summaries.Q20127550: Begun in 1754 outside the walls by the architect Isaac Guidais, this folie was, barely completed, threatened with demolition for the building of the allées basses of the Peyrou; the bishop of Nîmes opposed it. Ferdinand de Hompesch, grand master of the Order of Malta, settled there in the hope that the faculty of medicine would cure the illness he died of in 1805.
summaries.Q3076244: Carved by Étienne Dantoine for the place de la Canourgue, this marble group was completed in 1776, but a dispute with the municipality delayed its installation. It reached the place de la Comédie in 1793. The damaged original was removed in 1989 and replaced by a resin cast; the marble stands in the foyer of the Opéra Comédie.
summaries.Q63762464: Decided as early as November 1918 and inaugurated on 6 May 1923, this monument by the architect Jacques-Léon Février takes the form of a semicircular Corinthian colonnade. An underground ambulatory bears the names of more than 2,200 soldiers from the commune. Erected in the centre of the jardin de l’Esplanade, it was moved in 1993 during the building of the Corum.
summaries.Q3399123: Also called the Vieille porte, it is a remnant of the fortified wall that protected Montpellier in the late 12th and early 13th centuries, which had twenty-five towers. With the tour de la Babote, the porte du Pila Saint-Gély and the tour des Pins, it is one of its last surviving traces. Listed as a historic monument in 1938.
summaries.Q3100546: Founded in 1593 by Pierre Richer de Belleval under letters patent from Henri IV to grow “simples”, or medicinal plants, it is the oldest botanical garden in France, ahead of the one in Strasbourg (1619). The garden was wiped out during the siege of the city in 1622 and Richer had to start all over again. It covers 4.6 hectares.
summaries.Q3407377: Decided in 1688 by the city council at the highest point of Montpellier, the promenade was inaugurated in 1690. The 4.59-hectare esplanade brings together the triumphal arch, the equestrian statue of Louis XIV and the water tower fed by the aqueduc Saint-Clément. The king stretches out his arm there: supposed to point to Spain, it in fact points to Italy.
summaries.Q144375: Built from 1753 to 1765 under the direction of the engineer Henri Pitot, it brought water to the water tower of the Peyrou. Pitot took his inspiration from the pont du Gard: two superimposed rows of arches, the short span of the small ones reducing the risk of cracking. The initial flow of 25 litres per second reached 250 l/s after the underground doubling of 1931.
summaries.Q58480511: Built in 1691 at the same time as the triumphal arch and by the same architect, Augustin-Charles d’Aviler, this stone bridge replaced the old drawbridge and links the rue Foch to the esplanade du Peyrou. Called the pont du Peyrou, it was renamed in honour of Louis Vialleton after his death in 1929.
summaries.Q1065164: It owes its name to the municipal theatre, burnt down in 1785 and again in 1881 and rebuilt each time, whose façade adorns the south-west side. The first square dates from 1755, on the former site of the city wall. The fontaine des Trois Grâces, by Étienne Dantoine, was installed there in the late 1790s.
summaries.Q80564925: Its name comes from Occitan: the land belonged to the chapter of Saint-Pierre, and “canourgue” means a canonical chapter. The square took shape after work on a new cathedral was abandoned, halted in 1629 on the orders of Richelieu, who preferred to have Saint-Pierre restored. The hôtel Richer de Belleval housed the town hall there from 1816 to 1975.
summaries.Q3390640: The site was home to the Capuchin convent, destroyed during the Revolution. A statue of Louis XVI was installed there in 1829, ten years after the laying of the first stone, then taken down and put into storage in 1831 after the advent of the July Monarchy; in 1966 the mayor François Delmas gave it to Louisville, Montpellier’s twin city.
summaries.Q3389884: The square occupies the void left by the demolition in 1794 of the church of Notre-Dame-des-Tables, which owed its name to the money changers established in front of its walls in the 12th century. Its crypt, left intact beneath the halls of 1806, houses the museum of the history of Montpellier. Jaurès had spoken there during the winegrowers’ revolt of 1907.
summaries.Q3447920: Laid out in 1205 with the second city wall, it led to the porte du Peyrou and bore its name until 1860. Cut through and widened in the Haussmann spirit under mayor Jules Pagézy, it became rue Impériale in 1864, then rue Nationale under the Third Republic; the works stopped in 1885 for lack of money. It took the name of Marshal Foch in 1929.
summaries.Q3451463: In the Middle Ages its Occitan name “carrièira daurada”, golden street, came from the goldsmiths and silversmiths established there. Its name comes from the Grande Loge des marchands, built around 1447 by Jacques Cœur at the corner of the rue de l’Aiguillerie and since destroyed. Before the place de la Comédie was created in 1755, it opened onto the porte de Lattes.
summaries.Q3451177: A pedestrian shopping street in the Écusson, at its southern end it meets the place Jean-Jaurès and the rue de la Loge. Its name refers to the needle makers once established there: in Montpellier the trade has disappeared, the street name has remained. It is home to bars and shops that are alternative, ecological or devoted to foreign cultures.
summaries.Q102293279: The street runs along the place de la Canourgue and owes its name to the church of Sainte-Croix, the castle chapel of the second castle of the Guilhem, lords of Montpellier. A revolt of his subjects forced Guilhem VI to abandon that castle and build another. Having become the property of the cathedral canons, the church was destroyed by the Protestants in 1621.
summaries.Q58426872: This street links the place de la Comédie to the place Auguste-Gibert and the gare Saint-Roch. Closed to car traffic since 1986, it is crossed by tramway lines 1 and 2. It runs alongside the square Planchon, laid out in 1858, and the Protestant temple, inaugurated in 1870.
summaries.Q3058438: An extension of the place de la Comédie, the esplanade was born of the dismantling of the ramparts: the walls were pulled down and the ditch filled in in 1679, leaving a carriage road. The duc de Roquelaure had a promenade laid out there in 1723 and the following year. The jardin du Champ-de-Mars, sold by the army to the City, became an esplanade in 1900.
summaries.Q16670337: In Occitan, plan means a square: this triangular one appeared after 1862 in the Figuerolles district with the demolition of the buildings of the île Verdier. A daily market has been held there since 1924, at first specialising in firewood. Closed in 2006, it was reinstated in 2016, six mornings a week.
summaries.Q2922064: This thoroughfare borders the Écusson and takes its name from jeu de paume, a ball game widely played in Languedoc. Three years of works were needed to pedestrianise it and run tramway line 4 along it. At no. 30 the deaf-mute painter Frédéric Peyson died, on 13 January 1877.
summaries.Q3390528: This square in the historic heart owes its name to the resistance fighters and political opponents honoured after the Allied victory. During the Second World War, the prefecture that stands there was the meeting place of the Pétainist leaders and the transit point for those opponents before their imprisonment or deportation.
summaries.Q3452508: In the Écusson, the street links the rue de l’Aiguillerie to the place du Corum. “Pila Saint Gély” is the Occitan name of the former faubourg Pile Saint-Gilles. At no. 27 stands the Logis du Chapeau-Rouge, an inn renowned as early as the 16th century, whose construction began in the 13th.
summaries.Q58650777: Inaugurated in 1880 by mayor Alexandre Laissac, the iron and cast-iron market hall was nicknamed the “marché bas”. Demolished in 1966, it gave way in 1968 to a concrete hall topped by a car park, the “marché rond”. Razed in turn in 2016, it was replaced by a metal and glass building inaugurated on 1 December 2018.
summaries.Q3395579: The shopping centre owes its name to the military land used there for artillery and shooting practice. Inaugurated on 5 March 1975 by mayor François Delmas, it opened with 34,000 m2 and the Galeries Lafayette, which left the place de la Comédie at that point. A second floor was added in 1996, and the renovation with its glass roof was inaugurated in 2021.
summaries.Q801197: Built in 1844, the station owes its location to the military, who opposed the straight route that the engineer Didion wanted to run across the Esplanade. With the TGV approaching, in 1980, everything was demolished and rebuilt except the façade, the central part of which has been listed as a historic monument since 1984.
summaries.Q3268766: Inaugurated on 7 March 1804 under the name of Grand Lycée impérial, the school followed on from the royal college founded by the Jesuits in 1629, which occupied the premises of the present musée Fabre. In 1947 it was moved into the citadel built from 1624 to 1627 under Louis XIII, and shortly afterwards took the name of lycée Joffre.
summaries.Q2853220: Designed from 1978 by the Catalan architect Ricardo Bofill at the instigation of mayor Georges Frêche, the district was built from 1983 on land occupied until then by a military shooting range, an association and an industrial wasteland. Its postmodern style combines fluted columns and tinted concrete imitating stone.
summaries.Q2969230: Étienne de Flaugergues, a councillor at the Cour des comptes of Montpellier, bought the estate in 1696 and embellished it for nearly half a century. Passed down by inheritance and never sold, the folie belongs to the Colbert family. Its staircase with hanging keystones rises three storeys without the support of a single pillar.
summaries.Q2014804: This area devoted to leisure and retail, in the Port Marianne district, was built on land still farmed in the late 1990s: the Gaumont multiplex in 1998, the Végapolis ice rink in 2000, the Galilée planetarium in 2002, the Mare Nostrum aquarium in 2007. The shopping centre opened on 24 September 2009.
summaries.Q59279414: Built in 1845 in the rue des Étuves by the architect Omer Lazard, this chapel is in the neo-Gothic troubadour style. An organ from the Théodore Puget workshop was added in 1891; Albine de Montholon is buried in the crypt.
summaries.Q3145748: Erected between 1669 and 1682 by Charles de Boulhac, a councillor at the cour des comptes, the mansion was bought by the city in 1816 to become the town hall, a role it kept until 1975. After major works, it reopened in June 2021: a luxury hotel, a gastronomic restaurant and a contemporary art foundation.
summaries.Q59164849: Founded in 1678 and built in 1680 on the site of the former Carmelite convent, the general hospital wanted by Louis XIV served to confine, feed and treat beggars and vagrants. Closed gradually between 1970 and 1997, it became the Saint-Charles campus of the université Paul-Valéry, delivered in two phases in 2011 and 2017.
summaries.Q832351: Erected in 1691 by Augustin-Charles d’Aviler, architect of the province of Languedoc, from drawings by François II d’Orbay, this arch 15 metres high and 18 wide gave access to the Peyrou. In 1694 Philippe Bertrand made four medallions there, one of which depicts the joining of the two seas by the canal royal de Languedoc.
